query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Substituting conventional dipping and plating components with a refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) will reduce erosion in hot‐dip aluminum plating equipment because its elevated melting point and tendency to form stable protective oxides will shield the substrate from direct attack by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk, homogeneous RHEA (e.g., an alloy based on refractory elements such as Nb, Ta, Ti, and V) in an as‐fabricated, defect-controlled state.
generation.intervention: Replace standard equipment parts (such as rollers and guide plates) with RHEA-based parts prepared to specifications for high-temperature operation.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures near or slightly above 660°C during hot-dip plating cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable, refractory oxide layer (e.g., oxides of Nb and Ta) on the RHEA surface that limits further aluminum attack.
generation.mechanism: The inherent high melting point and chemical inertness of refractory elements in the alloy promote formation of a protective oxide scale. This scale serves as a barrier that minimizes corrosive interactions between the metal substrate and liquid aluminum, thereby reducing erosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: RHEA components will exhibit significantly lower rates of erosion (and thus extend service life) compared to conventional materials such as carbon or alloy steels, when subjected to the same hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional hot-dip plating equipment parts (e.g., those made from carbon or alloy steel) show severe erosion and reduced service life due to prolonged exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the protective oxide layer and overall corrosion resistance may depend on the precise alloy composition, processing history, and thermal cycling conditions. Under extreme or fluctuating thermal/mechanical stresses, the protective behavior might be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: Although refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit promising mechanical and high-temperature stability properties, there is limited experimental data specifically on their corrosion rates and protective oxide behavior in molten aluminum environments. Detailed empirical evaluation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of dipping/plating equipment components: one set made from a conventional material (e.g., alloy steel) and one set made from the selected RHEA. Expose both sets to a controlled molten aluminum bath at plating temperatures for a prolonged period, with periodic extraction for analysis.
measurements: Measure mass loss and surface erosion using microscopy and weight-loss techniques.
Characterize the composition and integrity of surface oxide scales via XPS or EDS.
Assess mechanical integrity post-exposure by hardness tests and bend tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA parts do not exhibit a significantly lower erosion rate (e.g., reduced mass loss, shallower corrosion penetration) or if their protective oxide scale dissolves or degrades faster than that on conventional materials under identical conditions, then the hypothesis—that RHEA components improve erosion resistance in molten aluminum—is falsified.

Question: How does varying the mechanical alloying milling time affect the microstructural evolution, phase composition, contamination levels, and mechanical properties of the Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) produced via powder metallurgy?. System: Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA). Processing: Mechanical alloying in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill under high-purity argon (99.9999%) using hardened steel balls (AISI 52100, 15 mm diameter) at 250 RPM with a 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio; subsequent consolidation via spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 50 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 °C·min⁻¹ heating rate, and 15 min dwell time.. Test conditions: Milling times of 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 hours; sintering of powders milled for 3, 10, 30, and 50 hours; microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness (0.2 kgf load), nanoindentation (100 mN max load), and ultrasound methods..
